label: verify-t6-flyingfish-crit

claims.claim: M3 stall-floor bound is exceeded by lofted launches (13-58% for printed glider, 7.5-12 m/s); P5 1.10 cannot absorb it; no-floor bound held in every case.
claims.source_says: printed glider v0=7.5: ratio x/M3=1.58, x/noFloor=0.57; v0=12: ratio x/M3=1.13, x/noFloor=0.80. Registry scope: "A single steady glide with no thrust and lift equal to weight"
claims.note: Printed outputs match the claim and the registry quote is exact; these are the agent's own simulation results and I did not rerun the script.

claims.claim: P2 cannot fail independently of P1: ratio>1 needs v0<13.77, P1 demands v0>=16.09, and the 0.30 floor corresponds to v0=25.13 m/s.
claims.source_says: Abstract: "the flying fish can achieve a distance up to 45.4 m, and reach a height of 13.2 m". I recomputed sqrt(2g*45.4/4.7)=13.77 and sqrt(2g*45.4/(4.7*0.3))=25.13; sqrt(2g*13.2)=16.09.
claims.note: Arithmetic reproduces and the Europe PMC abstract confirms 45.4 m and 13.2 m; the P2 ratio form comes from the design file, which I did not open.

claims.claim: P3 0.50 s threshold is only 20% above ballistic time in its extreme case and is exceeded by angle error alone (0.632 s at 30 deg, the field angle in the project data).
claims.source_says: recompute.out: v 5.15 th 23.3: T_M5 0.500 T_ballistic 0.415; th 30: T_M5 0.632. takeoff-data.csv: "previous field studies cited there give about 30 deg"
claims.note: 0.500/0.415 is 1.205, and the 30 deg value is in the data file; the 0.632 s is the model time with lift, not a measured time.

claims.claim: P6 cannot fail on 1.8.1: the 1.7.0 fix made the checker return out-of-scope for declared glides and added a standing test.
claims.source_says: CHANGELOG 1.7.0: "the checker now returns out-of-scope for a declared unpowered glide, and a standing registry test asserts no accepted law is violated by a real organism making a realistic claim."
claims.note: Quote is verbatim and browser-check.mjs line 1828 returns out-of-scope for E3 when fm.unpowered; whether that makes P6 unfailable is partly the agent's inference.

overall: All four key claims hold up against the sources I could read: the simulation outputs, the arithmetic, the data file, the changelog quote and the Europe PMC abstract. The simulations are the agent's own and I did not rerun them.
